/Friday through Tuesday/... 
Friday is still looking like a fairly wet day across the bulk of 
central Arizona as moisture levels rise to near 200-250% of normal 
under strong low level moisture advection, while simultaneously 
situated under strong difluence aloft in the left front quadrant of 
the incoming near record strength (for this time of year) 
subtropical jet. Guidance continues to heavily favor showers and 
isolated thunderstorms developing Friday morning centered over south-
central Arizona, then expanding north and east throughout the day. 
Rainfall rates may not be particularly heavy with the bulk falling 
at less than 0.25"/hour, however embedded heavier showers and/or 
thunderstorms with rates 0.50-1.00"/hour may be possible. 

GEFS and EPS ensemble mean QPF for the Friday event shows an average 
of around 0.25"-0.75" from Phoenix and into the higher terrain north 
and northeast of Phoenix to 0.10-0.25" over much of the rest of 
southern and central Arizona. The higher end of guidance (NBM 75% 
percentile) still shows potential for heavy rainfall with amounts of 
up 1.00"-1.50" across south-central Arizona, albeit more tied to 
convective elements, and likely not widespread. As a result, WPC's 
ERO continues to depict a Slight Risk for excessive rainfall on 
Friday. Given the propensity for these higher end NBM QPF 
probabilities to subjectively be overzealous in mid range forecasts 
over lower elevations, the ensemble means would be more favored over 
larger area. Nevertheless, some higher end amounts of over 1" 
should be expected in more convectively dominated areas, but these 
type of totals are likely to be fairly localized. 

As one portion of the subtropical jet and embedded shortwave lifts 
northeast late Friday, the best ascent will shift out of Arizona 
leaving lesser rainfall chances, and tied more towards isolated 
upslope driven shower activity Friday night and Saturday. Models 
continue to highlight a distinct break in rainfall Saturday before 
the unsettled pattern returns Saturday night and Sunday with an 
atmospheric river approaching the region. The majority of modeling 
suggests the brunt of this expected modest atmospheric river 
impacting areas across southern Arizona and northern Sonora. While 
the overall trend in ensembles continues to depict mean troughing 
advancing through the SW Conus, uncertainty remains quite high 
regarding some very important details regarding the track, strength, 
phasing, and orientation of the southern stream shortwave trough 
yielding substantial differences in the amount of moisture that may 
be thrust inland by the atmospheric river. 

Large differences in output continue to be exhibited among each 
iteration of operational and ensemble members with the key being the 
ability for deep southwest flow at lower latitudes to become 
juxtaposed with the atmospheric river in order for moisture to 
breach the terrain gap in the Baja peninsula. Given the continued 
wide range in solutions, it may be a couple more days to reach a 
better consensus. Overall, both GEFS and EPS members continue to 
show wide ranges from nearly no accumulations across lower 
elevations to well over 2 inches. Realistically, the GEFS mean 0.25-
0.50" for south-central Arizona looks to be a bit too low 
considering the potential amount of moisture, but the EPS mean 0.75-
1.50" may be a bit too high and a symptom of grid spacing bleeding 
greater high terrain amounts into lower elevations. Regardless, the 
bulk of the rain should fall throughout the day Sunday (which could 
be a rare "wash-out" day for some locations), but as stated above, 
how much total rain will fall is still quite uncertain. Considering 
this will be the second rain event within 3 days, any additional 
moderate to heavy rain could compound any flooding issues that occur 
Friday. Rain chances may linger through Sunday night across eastern 
Arizona, but by Monday, much of the area should be drying out as the 
system is quickly pushes east of the area.

Temperatures during this unsettled weather pattern will fall below 
normal starting Friday with highs dropping to between 75F-80F before 
bottoming out closer to 70F highs for Sunday and/or Monday. It would 
not be out of the question for some lower desert communities stuck 
in prolonged rain Sunday to not even breach the 70F threshold. NBM 
guidance shows fairly large forecast temperature spread for the 
first half of next week as the large scale troughing may linger near 
the region with depressed H5 heights for a couple more days. If this 
happens, highs will very slowly creep upward through the low to mid 
70s, whereas if the ridge quickly takes over, highs closer to 80F 
would be more common by next Tuesday or Wednesday.
